name: URL Shortener
description: Classic read-heavy cache-aside pattern with PostgreSQL + Redis. Demonstrates cache hit/miss ratios, DB query amplification on cache miss, and strategy tradeoffs.
descriptionLite: Classic read-heavy cache-aside with PostgreSQL + Redis on a single app server. Demonstrates cache hit/miss ratios, DB query amplification on cache miss, and strategy tradeoffs.

variations.label: App, cache, and database
variations.description: Cache-aside Redis. App reads Redis first, falls back to Postgres.

variations.label: App, proxy cache, and database
variations.description: Caching proxy between app and Postgres. No direct app-to-database edge.

cache.base: Redis holds short code to URL mappings

variants.label: SET hits Redis first; the caching proxy writes Postgres before ack. On miss, the proxy loads from Postgres and refills Redis (read-through is always on).
SET lands in Redis; the proxy flushes Postgres later. On miss, the proxy loads from Postgres and refills Redis (read-through is always on).
App checks Redis; on miss it reads Postgres and SETs the key

db.base: Postgres table mapping codes to original URLs

app-server-\u003ecache.base: App checks Redis for short:{code} on the hot resolve path.

variants.label: App talks to the caching proxy: SET writes Redis then Postgres before ack; GET miss fills from Postgres (read-through).
App talks to the caching proxy: SET lands in Redis and flushes Postgres later; GET miss fills from Postgres (read-through).
App GETs Redis first; on miss it reads Postgres and SETs the key.

app-server-\u003edb.base: App looks up original URLs in Postgres on cache miss (and writes new codes).

cache-\u003edb.base: Proxy cache fills or flushes against Postgres for this strategy.

lb-\u003eapp-server.base: Load balancer spreads HTTP to app-server replicas.

journeys.label: Resolve short URL

steps.action: GET short:{code} ; hot path for popular links.
steps.lesson: Most traffic should stop here. A hit avoids Postgres on the read path.

steps.action: SELECT original URL by code when cache misses.
steps.detail: SELECT url FROM urls WHERE code = ?
steps.lesson: Cache-aside miss: the app loads the row and can warm Redis for the next GET.

steps.action: On miss, the caching proxy runs configured SQL, repopulates the key, then returns the URL to the app.
steps.detail: Proxy-driven SELECT + backfill (read-through, always on in proxy mode)
steps.lesson: Proxy miss-fill: your app never talks to Postgres on reads. The caching proxy owns the load.

journeys.explanation: Classic cache-aside: try Redis for the mapping, fall back to Postgres on miss.

explanationVariants.text: Write-through: every write lands in Redis then Postgres before ack, so fresh codes stay warm. On miss, the proxy still loads from Postgres and refills Redis (read-through is always on).
Write-behind: new codes appear in Redis immediately while Postgres persistence trails. On miss, the proxy loads from Postgres and refills Redis (read-through is always on).

journeys.label: Create short URL

steps.action: Allocates a code, persists the mapping, returns short URL.
No Redis write on create; the next GET /r/{code} miss warms the cache.
steps.lesson: Cache-aside here does not SET on write; codes are immutable, so the first resolve populates Redis.

steps.action: SET short:{code}; caching proxy persists to Postgres before completing the write.
steps.lesson: Write-through: Redis accepts first; the proxy persists to Postgres before the write completes so later GETs stay warm. On DB failure the proxy deletes the cache key.

steps.action: Row written via caching-proxy after Redis accept.
SET short:{code}; proxy acknowledges immediately; durable INSERT is asynchronous.
INSERT applied asynchronously by the caching-proxy after the hot write path.

journeys.explanation: Cache-aside write path: insert into Postgres; Redis is populated on the first successful resolve.

explanationVariants.text: Write-through: the app writes to the proxy; Redis is set first and Postgres is persisted synchronously before the write completes (with cache rollback if the DB write fails).
Write-behind: Redis accepts SET immediately for low latency; the proxy flushes the row to Postgres in the background (brief window where Redis is ahead of durable storage).

cache_hit_low.cause: More lookups are missing Redis and falling through to Postgres.

db_latency.cause: URL lookups hit Postgres directly on cache miss.
db_latency.suggestion: Add a cache node to serve hot lookups from Redis.

name: E-Commerce
description: Multi-server product catalog with shared database and cache layer. Tests load balancer distribution and write contention. Add a message queue and worker for async order processing.
descriptionLite: Product catalog with shared PostgreSQL and Redis cache on a single app server. Catalog reads benefit from cache; checkout writes contend on the database.

variations.label: App and database
variations.description: Direct Postgres catalog and checkout. No cache or async worker.

variations.label: App, cache, and database
variations.description: Sync catalog with cache-aside Redis. Checkout writes hit Postgres directly.

variations.label: App, cache, MQ, worker, and database
variations.description: Async checkout with RabbitMQ worker and cache-aside catalog reads.

cache.base: App checks Redis for catalog and product keys; misses load from Postgres

worker.base: Consumes orders from the queue and runs fulfillment

app-server-\u003ecache.base: App checks Redis for catalog and product keys (cache-aside).

app-server-\u003edb.base: App reads catalog/inventory and writes orders directly to Postgres.

app-server-\u003emq.base: Checkout publishes order.placed for async fulfillment.

lb-\u003eapp-server.base: Load balancer spreads HTTP to app-server replicas.

worker-\u003edb.base: Worker updates order/fulfillment state in Postgres.

worker-\u003emq.base: Fulfillment worker consumes order.placed from this queue.

journeys.label: Catalog browse
journeys.explanation: Catalog GET checks Redis first. On miss the app loads from Postgres and SETs the key. Checkout always writes inventory and orders to Postgres directly.

journeys.label: Checkout
journeys.explanation: Writes hit Postgres; optional MQ/worker handle async fulfillment.

db_latency.cause: Checkout and catalog paths contend on shared Postgres under load.
db_latency.suggestion: Add cache or read replicas to spread read load; scale workers if the queue backs up.

name: Social Feed (Push)
description: Fan-out on write: new posts are pushed to every follower's pre-computed feed via a message queue and worker. Reads are O(1) but writes create amplification. Demonstrates consumer lag, backpressure, and queue depth under load.
descriptionLite: Fan-out on write without a queue: the app pushes new posts into follower timelines in Redis. Reads are O(1) from sorted sets; POST pays sync fan-out cost on the app server.
bottleneckLite: Sync fan-out on POST scales with follower count

variations.label: Sync push timeline
variations.description: App writes follower timelines in Redis on each post. No message queue.

variations.label: Async push timeline
variations.description: App publishes to a queue. Workers fan out timeline updates to Redis.

app-server.base: Handles post creation and feed reads

variants.label: Pull mode: every feed read runs a DB JOIN
Fans out new posts in-process; serves feeds from Redis
Publishes new posts to the queue; serves feeds from Redis

cache.base: Pre-computed user timeline cache (Redis sorted sets)

variants.label: Written by the fan-out worker after consuming from the queue
Written synchronously by app-server on each post

db.base: Stores users, posts, and the follower graph

mq.base: Buffers new posts before fan-out to followers

worker.base: Consumes posts from the queue, writes to follower timelines

variants.label: No Redis target for fan-out writes

app-server-\u003ecache.base: App reads follower timelines from Redis (ZREVRANGE on timeline:{userId}).

variants.label: No Redis on the canvas — feed reads fall back to Postgres JOINs.

app-server-\u003edb.base: App reads and writes users, posts, and the follower graph in Postgres.

app-server-\u003emq.base: App publishes new posts to the queue for async fan-out.

lb-\u003eapp-server.base: Load balancer spreads HTTP to app-server replicas.

worker-\u003ecache.base: Worker writes timeline:{followerId} sorted sets in Redis after each post.

worker-\u003edb.base: Worker loads follower lists and post metadata from Postgres.

worker-\u003emq.base: Fan-out worker consumes post events from this queue.

journeys.label: Feed reads

steps.detail: Redis sorted set lookup, sub-ms when warm.
steps.lesson: Push read path: twenty newest posts from a pre-built timeline. Score is post time; no JOIN when the zset is warm.

steps.detail: SELECT ... WHERE follower_id = ? ORDER BY created_at DESC
steps.condition: If Redis empty or no cache
steps.lesson: Optional miss path when the timeline key is empty. Strict push mode usually returns an empty feed instead of falling back here.

steps.action: 3-table JOIN: posts, follows, users. Returns top 20 by timestamp.
steps.detail: SELECT p.* FROM posts p JOIN follows f ON f.followed_id = p.user_id WHERE f.follower_id = $1 ORDER BY p.created_at DESC LIMIT 20
steps.lesson: Pull mode: every GET runs this JOIN. Latency tracks how many accounts you follow, not how many posts landed in Redis ahead of time.

journeys.explanation: In push mode, most warm reads hit Redis. Without cache, every read does a 3-table JOIN.

explanationVariants.text: Pull mode: every feed request runs a 3-table JOIN across posts, follows, and users. Latency grows with follower count since there's no pre-computed timeline to read from.

Sync push (no queue): timelines live in Redis like async push, but the app-server loads followers and ZADDs on each post instead of a worker. Reads stay cheap; POST still pays for follower lookup on the app.

journeys.label: Create post

steps.lesson: The client gets 202 after Postgres and a successful publish. Timeline writes happen later on workers, not on this HTTP thread.

steps.action: Consume from queue, fetch followers from DB.
steps.lesson: Each message triggers a follower query and a batch of ZADDs. Queue depth and worker count decide how fast timelines catch up.

steps.action: ZADD to timeline:{followerId} for each follower.
steps.lesson: One post becomes N sorted-set updates. That write amplification is the cost of O(1) feed reads later.

steps.action: App-server does sync ZADD to follower timelines.
steps.detail: Fire-and-forget goroutine, does not block response.
steps.lesson: Sync push: the app loads followers before it responds, then ZADD runs in a goroutine. Reads still hit Redis; POST latency still scales with follower count.

journeys.explanation: With RabbitMQ, the app inserts the post, publishes one message, and returns 202 once the broker accepts it. A worker loads followers from Postgres and ZADDs each timeline. Your client never waits on Redis.

explanationVariants.text: Sync push (no queue): the app inserts the post, loads followers from Postgres, and ZADDs each timeline in a goroutine before returning 200. Reads stay cheap in Redis; POST latency still scales with follower count.

cache_hit_low.cause: Sorted-set timelines are not classic cache-aside GET/SET; a low hit share can mean cold timelines, eviction under memory pressure, or traffic patterns that rarely reuse keys.
cache_hit_low.suggestion: Add Redis memory or shard timelines across more capacity so follower timelines stay resident under fan-out load.

cascade_cache_db.cause: When timeline freshness or eviction shifts what is resident in Redis, read paths can lean harder on Postgres even though the data model is push-oriented.
cascade_cache_db.suggestion: Add Redis memory or cache capacity if timelines are being evicted, or add read replicas if Postgres is the sustained bottleneck.

cascade_latency_miss.cause: For a Redis timeline store, rising latency with more misses often means timelines are cold or incomplete, so read paths do more work than a hot sorted-set lookup; when timelines are not materialized you also pay the full 3-table JOIN cost.
cascade_latency_miss.suggestion: Keep workers fed through MQ so timelines stay warm; add Redis memory or replicas if eviction is trimming hot keys.

cascade_mq_backpressure.suggestion: Add worker replicas and ensure the cache tier exists for the timeline store workers write into.

db_latency.cause: Feed reads that miss Redis do a 3-table JOIN (posts × follows × users), which is expensive as data grows.
db_latency.suggestion: Add MQ + worker nodes so timelines are precomputed into Redis; reads stay on sorted-set timelines instead of large joins.

mq_backpressure.cause: Each post fans out to ~{worker.fanout_size_p99} followers. At {mq.produce_rate} posts/s, workers deliver ~{worker.redis_write_rate} Redis writes/s.
mq_backpressure.suggestion: Add more worker replicas to increase fan-out throughput.

name: Social Feed (Pull)
description: Fan-out on read: feeds are generated on demand by joining posts and follows. Simple architecture but reads get expensive as follower counts grow. Compare with Push variant to see the tradeoff.
bottleneck: JOIN query latency scaling with follower count

variations.label: Pull feed (DB JOINs)
variations.description: Fan-out on read. Every feed request joins posts, follows, and users in Postgres.

app-server.base: GET /feed/{userId} and POST /post against Postgres only

variants.label: Pull mode: every feed read is a DB JOIN

db.base: Stores users, posts, and the follower graph

app-server-\u003edb.base: Every feed read and post write hits Postgres (pull / JOIN path).

lb-\u003eapp-server.base: Load balancer spreads HTTP to app-server replicas.

journeys.label: Feed reads

steps.detail: SELECT p.id, p.user_id, u.username, p.content, p.created_at FROM posts p JOIN follows f ON f.following_id = p.user_id JOIN users u ON u.id = p.user_id WHERE f.follower_id = $1 ORDER BY p.created_at DESC LIMIT $2
steps.lesson: Pull mode: every GET runs this JOIN. Latency tracks how many accounts you follow, not how many posts were pre-written to Redis.

steps.action: JOIN posts, follows, and users; return top 20 by created_at.
steps.detail: posts × follows × users — indexed on follower_id
steps.lesson: Postgres does the heavy work on each read. Under load, connection pool and JOIN cost dominate before you add cache or async fan-out.

journeys.explanation: Pull mode: every feed read hits Postgres with a multi-table JOIN. No Redis timeline means no cheap warm read path.

journeys.label: Create post

steps.detail: INSERT INTO posts (user_id, content) VALUES ($1, $2) RETURNING id, ...
steps.lesson: Pull writes only persist the row. Followers see the post on their next feed GET when the JOIN runs; there is no queue, worker, or timeline ZADD.
Inserts are cheap compared to fan-out-on-read. Write amplification shows up on GET /feed, not on POST /post.

journeys.explanation: POST /post is a single INSERT and 200 OK. Unlike push, nothing precomputes follower timelines; feed reads pay the JOIN cost later.

db_latency.cause: Every feed read performs a 3-table JOIN as follower counts grow.
db_latency.suggestion: Compare with the push template: add cache + MQ + worker to precompute timelines in Redis.
